meta.note: Objective checks have feedback for every option. Reflections show discussion points and are never graded.

items.prompt: A person is dreaming vividly during sleep. Which statement best fits the distinction drawn in this lesson?

options.text: They are not awake, yet they may be having experiences, so wakefulness and experience can come apart.
options.fb: Correct. Dreaming is a standard illustration that being awake and having experiences are different things.

options.text: They must be conscious in every sense, because dreams are experiences.
options.fb: Not quite. Dreams suggest experience, but the person is not awake or aware of the room, so some senses of the word do not apply.

options.text: They are unconscious in every sense, because they are asleep.
options.fb: Not quite. This ignores the experiential side. Whether dream experience counts is exactly the point of separating the senses.

items.explain: The lesson separates wakefulness from experience. Dreaming shows they can differ.

items.prompt: Select all of the following that the lesson presents as senses or aspects of 'conscious'.

options.text: Wakefulness
options.fb: Yes. A state of alertness as opposed to deep sleep or coma.

options.text: Awareness of a particular thing
options.fb: Yes. Noticing a sound or a feeling.

options.text: There being something it is like to have an experience
options.fb: Yes. Nagel's phrase for the sense most researchers find hardest.

options.text: Being intelligent
options.fb: No. The lesson treats intelligence as a separate topic. See the Lexicon for how the terms differ.

items.explain: Intelligence and consciousness are different ideas and the Lexicon treats them separately.

items.prompt: Block's distinction between phenomenal and access consciousness is best described as…

options.text: A proposal that information being available for report and control may be a different matter from how experience feels, which some researchers dispute.
options.fb: Correct. It is a proposal, and its status is contested.

options.text: A proven result that feeling and information processing are separate in the brain.
options.fb: No. The lesson says the distinction is debated, not proven.

options.text: A claim that animals have only one of the two.
options.fb: No. The distinction does not say that.

items.explain: It is a proposed distinction with continuing disagreement.

items.prompt: In your own words, explain why a claim that 'a system is conscious' needs a statement of which sense is meant.
points: Names at least two senses (for example wakefulness and experience).
Explains that evidence for one sense may not support the other.
Notes that experience is harder to test from outside.
Does not claim a single correct definition.
criteria: Did you name which sense you meant?
Did you give one example where two senses differ?

items.prompt: In Chalmers's framing, which of these is an 'easy' problem?

options.text: Explaining how the brain focuses attention on one stimulus.
options.fb: Correct. Functions like attention, discrimination and report are the 'easy' ones in his sense.

options.text: Explaining why there is something it is like to see red.
options.fb: That is the hard problem in his framing.

options.text: Explaining why the universe contains conscious beings at all.
options.fb: That is a still broader question and not the one the lesson contrasts.

items.explain: Functions are the 'easy' problems. Why they come with experience is the hard problem.

items.prompt: What is the best reading of Nagel's bat example?

options.text: Knowing how a mechanism works may not tell us what the experience is like for the creature that has it.
options.fb: Correct. It points to a gap in third-person description.

options.text: Bats are the only animals that are conscious.
options.fb: No. The example does not claim this.

options.text: Science can never study consciousness.
options.fb: No. The argument concerns a limit in one kind of explanation.

items.explain: The example is about a possible explanatory gap, not a ban on science.

items.prompt: A study relies on participants saying whether they saw a flash. Select the limitations this method has when studying experience.

options.text: A participant may have an experience they cannot or do not report.
options.fb: Yes. Report and experience can differ.

options.text: A participant may report an experience they did not have, for example from guessing or expectation.
options.fb: Yes. This is a known issue with report.

options.text: Reports can never be useful.
options.fb: No. Reports are useful. They are just not identical to experience.

options.text: The method measures access to information as much as experience.
options.fb: Yes. This is why researchers debate how to separate the two.

items.explain: Report is valuable evidence with known limits.

items.prompt: Explain in a few sentences what the hard problem is asking, and one reason a philosopher might doubt that it is a separate problem.
points: States the question as why functions are accompanied by experience.
Gives one skeptical reply, such as that explaining functions may leave nothing further to explain.
Presents both views as live positions.
criteria: Did you state the problem without answering it?
Did you present the skeptical view fairly?

items.prompt: What is the point of the contrastive method?

options.text: To compare brain activity when the same stimulus is and is not consciously perceived.
To compare people with large and small brains.
options.fb: No. It compares conditions, not people's brain sizes.

options.text: To show that people are always aware of everything in front of them.
options.fb: No. The method relies on the finding that they are not.

items.explain: It holds the stimulus constant and varies awareness.

items.prompt: A study finds that brain region X is more active on trials where participants reported seeing a stimulus. Which conclusion is best supported by this alone?

options.text: Region X activity is associated with reporting a stimulus, but it may reflect the report rather than the experience.
options.fb: Correct. The difference could reflect experience, report preparation, or both.

options.text: Region X is where consciousness is produced.
options.fb: Too strong. A difference does not show where consciousness is produced.

options.text: Region X plays no role in perception.
options.fb: Not supported. The study does not show this either.

items.explain: Correlation with report does not isolate experience.

items.prompt: If some stimuli can influence behaviour without being reported as seen, what follows?

options.text: Information processing and conscious perception are not identical.
options.fb: Correct. This is the lesson's conclusion, as reviewed by Dehaene and colleagues.

options.text: Consciousness is an illusion.
options.fb: No. That is a separate philosophical claim, not implied.

options.text: Behaviour is never influenced by what we see.

items.explain: Processing can occur without being reported as conscious.

items.prompt: Why does the lesson say that perception is 'not a window'? Give one example.
points: Mentions interpretation, expectation or filling-in.
Gives a concrete example such as an illusion or the blind spot.
Does not overclaim that perception is mere hallucination.
criteria: Did you separate the world from the experience of it?

items.prompt: Which description best fits attention as used in this lesson?

options.text: Selecting some information for fuller processing at the expense of other information.
Having a subjective experience.
options.fb: No. That describes awareness or experience.

options.text: Remembering the past.

items.explain: Attention is selection; awareness is a separate notion.

items.prompt: Koch and Tsuchiya argue that attention and consciousness…

options.text: Are different processes that may be separable, though the evidence is debated.
Are definitely identical.
Have nothing to do with each other.

items.explain: The claim is that they can come apart, with contested evidence.

items.prompt: Which pairing correctly states how a theory in the Theory Chamber relates attention to awareness?

options.text: Attention Schema Theory: awareness is the brain's simplified model of its own attention.
options.fb: Correct. This is how the theory is summarised by its proponents.

options.text: Attention Schema Theory: awareness is irrelevant to attention.
options.fb: No. The theory ties the two together.

options.text: Global Neuronal Workspace Theory: awareness is a simplified model of attention.
options.fb: No. That describes Attention Schema Theory, not GNWT.

items.explain: Different theories relate the two in different ways.

items.prompt: Explain why 'awareness requires attention' is a stronger claim than 'awareness and attention usually go together'.
points: Identifies that 'usually' allows exceptions while 'requires' does not.
Notes that one counterexample would challenge the stronger claim.
Mentions that the counterexamples are themselves disputed.
criteria: Did you point to what evidence would challenge each claim?

items.prompt: What does 'neural correlate of consciousness' name?

options.text: A pattern of brain activity that accompanies a particular conscious experience.
options.fb: Correct. The term does not claim to explain how the experience arises.

options.text: The part of the brain that creates consciousness.
options.fb: No. That claim goes beyond what the term says.

options.text: A device that measures consciousness.

items.explain: It names an accompanying pattern, not a cause.

items.prompt: Select the reasons that correlation with reported awareness may not identify the basis of experience.

options.text: The activity might be a prerequisite for experience rather than the experience itself.
The activity might be a consequence of experience, such as preparing to report.
Scientists have no way to record brain activity.
Different theories can interpret the same data differently.

items.explain: Association leaves open prerequisite, consequence and interpretation.

items.prompt: An adversarial collaboration agrees in advance what results would count against each theory. What is the main benefit?

options.text: It reduces the chance that each side reads ambiguous results as support for itself.
options.fb: Correct. Pre-agreed predictions make interpretation harder to bend.

options.text: It guarantees the correct theory will be found.
options.fb: No. It improves a test; it does not guarantee a winner.

options.text: It removes the need for brain recording.

items.explain: The design limits post-hoc interpretation.

items.prompt: Write two sentences: one on what an NCC finding can tell us, and one on what it cannot.
points: Can tell: which brain activity accompanies reported experience.
Cannot (alone): which activity produces experience, or why.
Notes interpretation depends on assumptions.
criteria: Did you avoid saying correlation shows cause?

items.prompt: Match each theory to its core idea.
pairs: Information amplified and broadcast across a network
Awareness as a model of attention
items.explain: These summaries follow the Theory Chamber's descriptions.

items.prompt: Why does the existence of many theories matter for how to read claims about consciousness?

options.text: It shows there is no agreed explanation, so confident claims that one theory is settled deserve scrutiny.
It shows consciousness does not exist.
options.fb: No. Disagreement about explanation does not remove the phenomenon.

options.text: It shows all theories are equally good.
options.fb: No. Evidence can favour some claims over others even when the field is unsettled.

items.explain: Unsettled field, so check the strength of any claim.

items.prompt: A news report says a theory was 'slammed as bogus science' in an open letter. What does the report show?

options.text: That a dispute exists. It is not itself a finding about the theory's truth.
options.fb: Correct. The report is secondary and the dispute is part of the field.

options.text: That the theory has been disproved.
options.fb: No. A letter is an argument, not an experiment.

options.text: That the theory is accepted by all scientists.

items.explain: The source record advises treating it as evidence of a dispute, not a finding.

items.prompt: Choose two theories and say, in a few sentences, what they treat as the key ingredient of consciousness.
points: States each theory's key ingredient accurately.
Notes how the ingredients differ.
Avoids saying which is right.
criteria: Did you describe each theory in terms its proponents would accept?

items.prompt: Which of these is presented as unresolved?

options.text: Whether consciousness can be measured objectively.
options.fb: Correct. It appears among the Archive's open questions.

options.text: Whether the brain exists.
Whether people use the word consciousness.

items.explain: Measurement and necessary neural processes remain open.

items.prompt: Why is a language model's statement 'I am conscious' weak evidence?

options.text: Such systems can generate fluent statements about experience from patterns in human language whether or not there is experience.
Machines cannot produce statements.
Humans never make false statements about experience.
options.fb: No, and that is not the point.

items.explain: The same output would be expected either way.

items.prompt: Select statements that accurately describe the indicator-property approach to AI consciousness described in the lesson.

options.text: It checks AI systems against properties drawn from scientific theories of consciousness.
The authors report that no current system was a strong candidate.
It proves that machines can never be conscious.
options.fb: No. It does not claim that.

options.text: It depends on the theories it draws from, which are themselves contested.

items.explain: The approach is useful and conditional.

items.prompt: Write a short paragraph on why 'we do not know' can be a responsible answer to a question about machine consciousness.
points: Explains that evidence and theory are unsettled.
Distinguishes 'unknown' from 'no'.
Mentions that overclaiming in either direction is a risk.
criteria: Did you avoid both overclaiming and dismissal?

items.prompt: A headline says 'Scientists prove where consciousness lives'. Which first question from the checklist is most useful?

options.text: Which sense of consciousness, what was measured, and does the evidence support the strength of the claim?
Is the headline well written?
options.fb: Style does not test the claim.

options.text: Has anyone shared it online?

items.explain: The checklist focuses on sense, measurement and strength.

items.prompt: Select statements consistent with this course.

options.text: Consciousness has several senses that should be kept apart.
Report is evidence about experience but is not identical to it.
A single theory has been accepted by all researchers.
Open questions should be presented as open.

items.explain: These summarise the course's main points.

items.prompt: Why does consciousness remain an active area of investigation?

options.text: There is no agreed explanation, and methods for testing theories are still developing.
Nobody has studied it.
It has been fully solved.

items.explain: Active because unsettled and under test.

items.prompt: Use the checklist on a claim about consciousness that you have recently read or heard. Write what you found.
points: Identifies the sense of consciousness.
Separates evidence from interpretation.
States what would change your mind.
criteria: Did you say what would count against the claim?

items.prompt: Which statement best describes how the term 'artificial intelligence' is used?

options.text: It names a research field and also the systems it produces, using many different methods.
It names one specific algorithm.
It names only systems that think like humans.
options.fb: No. Many AI systems are narrow and do not claim to think like people.

items.explain: AI is a field with several traditions.

items.prompt: Why might two researchers disagree about whether a system is 'intelligent'?

options.text: They may be using different definitions of intelligence.
options.fb: Correct. The definition shapes the test.

options.text: One of them must be mistaken about the facts.
options.fb: Not necessarily. The facts can be agreed while the definition differs.

options.text: Intelligence is not a topic anyone can discuss.

items.explain: Disagreement can be about the definition, not the facts.

items.prompt: Select the systems that the lesson implies are all called AI despite working differently.

options.text: A spam filter
A chess engine
A chatbot
A calculator that adds numbers
options.fb: Not discussed as AI here. Ordinary software is not usually called AI.

items.explain: The label covers varied methods.

items.prompt: Why might a news article that says 'AI decided' be too vague to evaluate?
points: Notes that AI covers many different systems.
Asks which system, trained on what, doing what.
Mentions that decisions involve people and design choices.
criteria: Did you ask what kind of system was involved?

items.prompt: Which event is generally treated as the naming moment of the field?

options.text: The 1955 Dartmouth proposal.
The 2017 transformer paper.
The 1986 back-propagation paper.

items.explain: The Dartmouth proposal used the phrase.

items.prompt: What is a key difference between rule-based and learning-based approaches?

options.text: Rule-based systems follow knowledge written down by people, learning systems adjust from examples.
Learning systems never use rules.
options.fb: No. The distinction is about where the behaviour comes from.

options.text: Rule-based systems are always more accurate.

items.explain: Where behaviour comes from differs.

items.prompt: A commentator says AI history shows a straight line to human-level minds. Which response is best supported by the lesson?

options.text: Different approaches succeeded at different tasks; the path to general intelligence is an open question.
They are certainly right.
options.fb: The lesson does not support this.

options.text: History has no relevance.
options.fb: No. History helps you judge such claims.

items.explain: The record is varied, not linear.

items.prompt: Explain one reason to be careful when someone says a new AI method is a 'breakthrough'.
points: Notes that results may be task-specific.
Mentions earlier cycles of enthusiasm.
Suggests checking what was actually tested.
criteria: Did you name what to check?

items.prompt: Which set lists the ingredients of a machine learning system?

options.text: Data, a model with adjustable parameters, a measure of error, and a procedure to reduce it.
A list of rules written by an expert and nothing else.
Only a very large computer.
options.fb: Computing power helps but is not the whole system.

items.explain: Data, model, error measure, adjustment.

items.prompt: A model has zero error on its training data but high error on the test set. What is the likely explanation?

options.text: It has overfit: it fits noise in the training data and does not generalise.
It has learned perfectly.
options.fb: No. Test error shows it has not generalised.

options.text: The test set is irrelevant.
options.fb: No. The test set is the check.

items.explain: Low training error with high test error indicates overfitting.

items.prompt: Match each kind of learning to its description.
pairs: Learns from examples with right answers
items.explain: These are the three standard families.

items.prompt: Why should a system be tested on data it was not trained on?
points: Explains that training data performance can be misleading.
Mentions generalisation.
Gives an example where leaked test data inflates results.
criteria: Did you explain what could go wrong without a test set?

items.prompt: Where is a trained network's behaviour stored?

options.text: In its weights, adjusted during training.
In a list of human-readable rules.
In a single special unit.

items.explain: Weights carry what was learned.

items.prompt: In the demonstration, a network with no hidden layer cannot learn XOR. Why?

options.text: A single layer can only separate inputs with a straight boundary, and XOR needs more.
XOR is too large a task.
options.fb: No. It is tiny. The limit is in what one layer can represent.

options.text: It was not trained long enough.
options.fb: Longer training does not fix a representational limit.

items.explain: Representational limit, not training time.

items.prompt: Which statement about learning in neural networks is accurate?

options.text: Training adjusts weights to reduce error on examples.
Training copies the brain's wiring.
Training gives the network consciousness.
options.fb: No. Nothing in the method implies this.

items.explain: Training is error-driven weight adjustment.

items.prompt: In your own words, describe how a network improves from its mistakes.
points: Mentions comparing output to the right answer.
Mentions adjusting weights to reduce error.
Mentions repetition over many examples.
criteria: Did you describe the loop of predict, compare, adjust?

items.prompt: What does a language model fundamentally do?

options.text: Predicts the probability of the next token given the preceding text.
Looks up the true answer in a database.
options.fb: Not by default. Some systems add retrieval, but prediction is the core mechanism.

options.text: Thinks about the meaning of each word as a human does.
options.fb: This claim goes beyond what the mechanism shows and is disputed.

items.explain: Next-token prediction is the core mechanism.

items.prompt: Select the reasons that fluent output from a language model can mislead.

options.text: Training aims at plausible text, not verified truth.
A model can state falsehoods confidently.
Fluent text is always accurate.
People tend to read fluent writing as evidence of understanding.
options.fb: Yes. This tendency is part of the concern critics raise.

items.explain: Fluency and accuracy come apart.

items.prompt: What is the role of human feedback in training an assistant-style model?

options.text: It shapes the model towards answers people judge better.
It makes the model conscious.
It removes the need for any other training.

items.explain: Feedback steers behaviour.

items.prompt: Explain the difference between a system that produces fitting text and one that understands. Say what evidence might distinguish them.
points: States that fitting output alone is compatible with both.
Suggests tests beyond fluent conversation.
Notes that the question is debated.
criteria: Did you propose evidence, not just assert a view?

items.prompt: What is a benchmark?

options.text: A standard set of tasks with agreed scoring used to compare systems.
A proof that a system is intelligent.
A kind of neural network.

items.explain: A benchmark is a shared test.

items.prompt: Select reasons that a high benchmark score may overstate ability.

options.text: The test may overlap with training data.
The model may exploit shortcuts.
The benchmark's name may promise more than it measures.
A high score always proves general ability.

items.explain: Scores are evidence with known weaknesses.

items.prompt: What does the lesson say about the debate over understanding in language models?

options.text: It is unresolved, in part because there is no agreed account of understanding.
It was settled in favour of one side.
It is meaningless.

items.explain: The debate is open.

items.prompt: Pick a benchmark you have heard of. What ability does it claim to measure, and how might a system score well without having that ability?
points: Names the claimed ability.
Describes a plausible shortcut.
Suggests a better check.
criteria: Did you separate the label from the skill?

items.prompt: Why are intelligence and consciousness treated as different questions?

options.text: Capability can be measured by tasks; experience cannot be read off from task performance.
Because they are the same thing.
Because machines are always conscious.

items.explain: Different kinds of evidence are involved.

items.prompt: What does Searle's Chinese Room argue?

options.text: That running a program is not by itself sufficient for understanding.
That no machine could ever do anything intelligent.
That all humans fail to understand.

items.explain: The target is sufficiency of running a program.

items.prompt: The indicator-property approach to AI consciousness is best described as…

options.text: A way to assess systems against properties drawn from scientific theories, whose conclusions depend on those theories.
A proof that current systems are conscious.
A test for intelligence.

items.explain: It is conditional on its theories.

items.prompt: Write a short response to the claim 'If it talks like it understands, it understands.'
points: Explains that behaviour is evidence but may not settle the question.
Mentions at least one competing view.
Notes the lack of consensus.
criteria: Did you acknowledge the strongest version of the opposing view?

items.prompt: Select limitations or risks named in this lesson.

options.text: Inaccuracy
Worse performance for groups under-represented in the data
Privacy concerns
Machines never make errors

items.explain: These are standard concerns.

items.prompt: What is a risk management framework for?

options.text: To give organisations a structured way to identify, assess and reduce harms.
To guarantee a system is safe.
options.fb: No, it does not guarantee safety.

options.text: To make AI conscious.

items.explain: A framework structures the work; it is not a guarantee.

items.prompt: Which question is listed as open?

options.text: Whether an artificial system could deserve moral consideration, and under what conditions.
Whether AI exists.
Whether people have used AI.

items.explain: This is in the Unanswered Archive.

items.prompt: Write a short account of one thing you understand about AI that you did not before, and one question that remains.
points: Names a specific idea from the course.
Raises a question that is open, not already settled.
Connects to evidence or a source.
criteria: Did you identify a question that cannot be answered by looking something up?
